newsitem.title: GREECE: Angry Greek farmers descend on Athens to protest.
newsitem.headline: Angry Greek farmers descend on Athens to protest.

text.p: Thousands of angry Greek farmers headed for Athens on Thursday to take their 22-day protest to parliament and demand a face-to-face meeting with Prime Minister Costas Simitis.
About 200 buses ferrying farmers from Greece's agricultural heartland in Thessaly were en route. Farmers' representatives said they would march through the capital to parliament.
"We will march to parliament and ask for a meeting with the prime minister. This is his chance to show that he cares about our problems," farmers' representative Vangelis Boutas said.

The farmers have blocked Greece's main roads for 22 days to press their economic demands. Simitis, who won elections in September, has refused to make concessions, saying the state had no more money to give.
Greek radio reporters with the convoy estimated that as many as 7,000 farmers were aboard and said more buses were joining as the caravan made its way to the capital.
Simitis has flatly rejected the farmers' demands for cheaper fuel, equipment and state subsidies on products, saying next year's budget cannot afford the cost estimated at $4 billion.

He has also ruled out meeting the farmers personally before they lift a three-week road blockade which has cost the economy more than $100 million. Police were building up their forces around Simitis's office in central Athens on Thursday.
Simitis has bluntly told the protesting farmers and workers from an array of sectors that there is no spare money for higher salaries, bonuses or pensions.
The farmers' march through Athens coincides with the debate in parliament on the 1997 budget, which ends with a vote on Saturday night.
Dozens of unions, representing teachers, seamen, public administrators and others, have joined in the farmers' direct challenge to the government.

They have stopped work briefly or gone on strike for one or two days in recent weeks to protest against tight incomes, a welter of higher direct and indirect taxes and the abolition of hundreds of tax exemptions by Simitis.
But Simitis has made few concessions and said that Greece's priority must be meeting European Union economic targets. He has said that sacrifices must be made, especially by the wealthy.
"If Mr Simitis doesn't meet us to discuss our demands we will go back to the barricades," Boutas said. "The government holds the key to end the blockade."
The number of barricades has dwindled in recent days in most parts of Greece but Thessaly farmers have stuck to a hard line and kept the main north-south road shut.
